name: Secondary Central Precocious Puberty in Male
aliases: Central Precocious Puberty Secondary to CNS Lesion in Males

diagnosticCriteria.formalCriteriaName: Consensus Criteria for Central Precocious Puberty

criteria.description: Development of secondary sexual characteristics before age 9 in males
Elevated basal or GnRH-stimulated luteinizing hormone (LH) and follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) levels consistent with pubertal activation
Neuroimaging evidence of central nervous system lesion or pathology triggering hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis activation
Radiologic evidence of advanced bone age compared to chronological age
Exclusion of peripheral causes of precocious puberty such as testicular tumors or adrenal disorders

diagnosticCriteria.minimumForDiagnosis: Presence of early pubertal development before age 9, elevated LH/FSH consistent with central activation, and neuroimaging evidence of CNS lesion
diagnosticCriteria.notes: Diagnosis requires exclusion of peripheral precocious puberty and confirmation of central activation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis.

pathognomonic.symptomName: Testicular enlargement consistent with pubertal development
Advanced bone age on radiographic assessment

occasional.symptomName: Visual field defects due to hypothalamic or pituitary mass effect
searchTerms: loss of side vision from brain mass
visual field loss due to pituitary tumor

occasional.symptomName: Nausea or vomiting secondary to increased intracranial pressure
searchTerms: vomiting caused by increased intracranial pressure
upset stomach linked to brain swelling
epileptic fits related to brain disorder

rare.symptomName: Hydrocephalus secondary to obstructive CNS lesion
Hypopituitarism symptoms due to mass effect

searchTerms: cranial nerve palsies causing facial or eye problems

laboratory: Elevated basal and GnRH-stimulated LH and FSH levels consistent with pubertal activation
Increased serum testosterone levels appropriate for pubertal stage
Normal or suppressed adrenal and peripheral sex steroid levels excluding peripheral causes
imaging: MRI of brain showing hypothalamic or pituitary lesions (e.g., hamartoma, glioma, astrocytoma)
genetic: No specific genetic mutations consistently identified; may be associated with syndromic CNS disorders
other: Growth velocity acceleration documented by serial height measurements

distinguishingFeatures: Elevated sex steroids with suppressed LH/FSH
Absence of CNS lesion on imaging
Presence of adrenal or testicular tumors or exogenous androgen exposure
No identifiable CNS lesion on neuroimaging

redFlags: Rapid progression of pubertal signs before age 9
Neurological symptoms such as persistent headache or visual disturbances
Signs of increased intracranial pressure (vomiting, papilledema)
references: Carel JC, Leger J. Precocious puberty. N Engl J Med. 2008;358(22):2366-2377.
Kaplowitz PB. Central precocious puberty: update on diagnosis and treatment. Horm Res Paediatr. 2016;85(2):79-85.
